questions.q: Your classmate says, “I’m sorry I broke your ruler.” What is a polite reply?
o: That’s all right; please be careful next time.
You are welcome to break it.
I don't know where the ruler is.
Please give me your homework.
questions.e: This reply accepts the apology and gives a gentle reminder.

questions.q: You need to know how to get to the library. What should you ask?
o: Could you borrow me the library?
Could you tell me how to get to the library?
Why did the library get here?
Do you have the library yesterday?
questions.e: “Could you tell me how to get to…?” is a polite way to ask for directions.

questions.q: A shopkeeper tells you the price. You think it is too high. What can you say politely?
o: Your price is foolish.
Give it to me for nothing.
Could you lower the price a little, please?
I will never look at it.
questions.e: A polite request can ask whether the seller can lower the price.

questions.q: Your friend invites you to a party, but you are busy. What is a polite reply?
o: I refuse your party forever.
Your party is not important.
I was there last week.
Thank you for inviting me, but I can’t come.
questions.e: Thank the person and explain briefly that you cannot come.

questions.q: Your friend has passed an important exam. What should you say?
o: Congratulations on passing your exam!
I’m sorry about your exam.
Good luck with your old exam.
Please pass me your exam.
questions.e: “Congratulations” is used to celebrate someone's success.

questions.q: You did not hear the last instruction. What should you ask?
o: Could you remove the instruction?
Could you repeat the last instruction, please?
Why did you speak yesterday?
I repeat your last instruction.
questions.e: Ask politely for the speaker to repeat what you missed.

questions.q: You meet your teacher at 8 a.m. What is an appropriate greeting?
o: Good night, sir.
See you yesterday, sir.
Good morning, sir.
Good evening tomorrow, sir.
questions.e: “Good morning” is used in the morning.

questions.q: You want to borrow your friend's dictionary. What should you say?
o: Could I lend your dictionary to you?
I borrowed your dictionary tomorrow.
Give me your dictionary now.
Could I borrow your dictionary for a moment?
questions.e: Use “Could I borrow…?” to ask to use something temporarily.

questions.q: You are speaking on the phone and cannot hear well. What can you say?
o: I’m sorry, the line is unclear. Could you speak more slowly?
The phone is speaking too much.
Please call the line slowly.
I cannot hear your color.
questions.e: This phrase explains the problem and politely asks the caller to slow down.

questions.q: You arrive late to class. What should you tell the teacher?
o: You are late because I am here.
I’m sorry I’m late. May I come in?
I will be late yesterday.
I don't come inside class.
questions.e: Apologize and ask permission to enter.

questions.q: A visitor asks where the nearest bus stop is. You know the way. What can you say?
o: It was a bus yesterday.
You need to ask the bus stop.
It’s just across the road, next to the pharmacy.
I am across the road last week.
questions.e: Give a clear location using familiar landmarks.

questions.q: You want to know whether a meal contains peanuts. What should you ask?
o: Did this dish contain a spoon?
Can this peanut eat the dish?
Is this dish beside the peanuts?
Does this dish contain peanuts?
questions.e: Ask directly whether the dish contains the ingredient.

questions.q: Your friend offers you tea, and you would like some. What should you say?
o: Yes, please. That would be lovely.
No, thank you; I am drinking it.
Yes, I refused yesterday.
Tea, you are welcome.
questions.e: “Yes, please” accepts an offer politely.

questions.q: You accidentally step on someone's foot. What should you say?
o: You should watch my foot.
I’m very sorry. Are you all right?
I am sorry for the weather.
Your foot is welcome.
questions.e: Apologize and check whether the person is okay.

questions.q: You want to leave a meeting early. What is a polite request?
o: I leave now; finish the meeting.
Will you leave me earlier?
Would it be all right if I left a little early?
I have been leaving yesterday.
questions.e: “Would it be all right if…?” is a polite way to ask permission.

questions.q: You do not understand a word in the lesson. What can you ask?
o: Why did this word go home?
What is the sentence doing?
How many words mean this?
What does this word mean in this sentence?
questions.e: Ask for the meaning of the unfamiliar word in context.

questions.q: Your classmate helps you carry books. What should you say?
o: Thanks for helping me carry these books.
You are welcome to carry my books.
I am sorry for your help.
Help me yesterday again.
questions.e: Thank the person for the help they gave.

questions.q: You disagree with a suggestion in a group. What is a respectful response?
o: Your idea makes no sense.
I see your point, but I have a different idea.
I agree, but I will not do it.
You are wrong, so stop talking.
questions.e: This phrase shows respect while expressing a different opinion.

questions.q: You want to ask a shopkeeper if a shirt comes in another size. What should you ask?
o: Can this shirt be more large?
Are you wearing another size?
Do you have this shirt in a larger size?
Did this shirt come yesterday?
questions.e: Ask whether the item is available in a different size.

questions.q: Your friend looks worried before an interview. What can you say?
o: You will fail before you begin.
You should cancel your interview.
I was sure yesterday.
I’m sure you’ll do well. Just be yourself.
questions.e: Offer encouragement and confidence.

questions.q: You want to check that you understood the meeting time. What can you say?
o: So, we’re meeting at three o’clock, right?
We met at three clocks, didn't we tomorrow?
Why is the meeting a clock?
I am meeting at three last week.
questions.e: A short confirmation question checks the information.

questions.q: Someone asks you to explain the route again. You are happy to help. What should you say?
o: No route is ever shown.
Of course. Let me show you on the map.
I already explained you.
The map will help me yesterday.
questions.e: “Of course” agrees to help, then offers a clear way to explain.

questions.q: You want to order food at a restaurant. What is a polite phrase?
o: I take the fish without asking.
Must I be the grilled fish?
Could I have the grilled fish, please?
The fish has me, please.
questions.e: “Could I have…?” is a polite way to order.

questions.q: Your classmate asks to use your notes. You agree but need them back tomorrow. What do you say?
o: No, take them forever.
I will use your notes tomorrow.
You can return my classmate.
Sure, you can use them. Please return them tomorrow.
questions.e: Accept and explain when you need the notes back.
